NYU Promise: meets 100% of demonstrated need for first-year students admitted to the New York campus, without the expectation of loans; families earning under $100,000 with typical assets pay no tuition

CSS Profile required for NYU scholarships (code 2785), plus FAFSA for US citizens/PRs (and NY TAP for NY residents). Due Nov 10 (ED I), Jan 10 (ED II), Feb 1 (RD); noncustodial parent Profile also required

Aid is need-based via the CSS Profile; no general merit scholarship application. A few selective named programs exist (e.g. MLK Scholars, Rudin Scholars for NYC public/parochial school students, Stern's Berkley Achievement Scholars)
$100,998 estimated 2026-27 cost of attendance (tuition and fees $68,576; food and housing $26,438; books $1,492; transportation $2,438; personal $2,054)
ED I (Nov 1) and ED II (Jan 1), both binding; RD Jan 5. No EA. Release from ED only if not admitted to your first-choice school/program/campus or aid is insufficient

One Common App covers New York, Abu Dhabi and Shanghai; you choose campus(es) and program(s) in the application. Tisch and some Steinhardt programs (e.g. Music, Studio Art) require an audition or portfolio, which can replace testing; submit the Common App a month early for these

One recommendation required (teacher, counselor, coach, supervisor or similar; up to three). Supplemental materials in the portal are usually due 1-2 weeks after the application deadline. $85 fee or waiver

supplements.label: NYU supplemental essay (optional)
supplements.prompt: We are looking for students who want to be bridge builders—students who can connect people, groups, and ideas to span divides, foster understanding, and promote collaboration within a dynamic, interconnected, and vibrant global academic community. We are eager for you to tell us how your experiences have helped you understand what qualities and efforts are needed to bridge divides so that people can better learn and work together. Please consider one or more of the following questions in your essay: (1) Tell us about a time you encountered a perspective different from your own. What did you learn—about yourself, the other person, or the world? (2) Tell us about an experience you’ve had working with others who have different perspectives. What role did you try to play in helping people to work together, and what did you learn from your efforts? (3) Tell us about someone you’ve observed who does a particularly good job helping people think or work together. How does this person set the stage for common exploration or work? What qualities do you admire in this person?
